method: OPEN AND QUOTED from American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review' (2023). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at PMC JATS XML <license> element for PMC10335308 (NCBI efetch; Europe PMC returned 503)). Source text: NCBI efetch JATS XML of the PMC author manuscript (Europe PMC fullTextXML returned HTTP 503 on 2026-09-23). Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from Table 1 (the four types) and Table 2 (testing and monitoring, with its footnotes).

claims.claim: **Consider testing women aged 15–50 with unexplained, recurrent severe abdominal pain** when an initial work-up has found no cause.
claims.source_text: Best Practice Advice 1: Women aged 15-50 years with unexplained, recurrent severe abdominal pain without a clear etiology after an initial workup should be considered for screening for an AHP.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Attacks cause neurovisceral symptoms:** severe abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, muscle weakness, neuropathy, tachycardia and hypertension.
claims.source_text: Clinically, they present with severe acute abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, muscle weakness, neuropathy, tachycardia, and hypertension.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **About 90% of symptomatic patients are women.** Most have only one or a few attacks in a lifetime; 3%–5% have recurrent attacks, usually defined as 4 or more a year.
claims.source_text: Approximately 90% of patients with symptomatic AHP are women and attacks are rare before onset of menses or after menopause in these patients. Among symptomatic patients with AHP, >90% experience only 1 or a few acute attacks in their lifetimes. … An estimated 3%-5% of patients with symptomatic AHP experience frequent recurrent attacks, typically defined as 4 or more attacks per year.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The four types (Table 1):** AIP, HCP and VP are autosomal dominant, present at 15–50 years and are commoner in women; HCP and VP can also affect the skin. ALAD porphyria is autosomal recessive, presents from childhood to adulthood and is commoner in men.
claims.source_text: [Table 1. row 1] AHP type: AIP · Inheritance: AD · Age at presentation: 15-50 y · Gender predominance: F > M · Symptoms and signs: Acute … [Table 1. row 2] AHP type: HCP · Inheritance: AD · Age at presentation: 15-50 y · Gender predominance: F > M · Symptoms and signs: Acute, cutaneous … [Table 1. row 3] AHP type: VP · Inheritance: AD · Age at presentation: 15-50 y · Gender predominance: F > M · Symptoms and signs: Acute, cutaneous … [Table 1. row 4] AHP type: ALAD · Inheritance: AR · Age at presentation: Childhood-adulthood · Gender predominance: M > F · Symptoms and signs: Acute … [Table 1. footnote] AD, autosomal dominant; AR, autosomal recessive; F, female; M, male.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **First test: a random (spot) urine for ALA, PBG, porphyrins and creatinine.** In an attack, ALA and PBG are at least 5 times the upper limit of normal, so a 24-hour collection is not needed.
claims.source_text: Best Practice Advice 2: Initial diagnosis of AHP should be made by biochemical testing measuring ALA, PBG, porphyrins, and creatinine in a random urine sample. … During acute attacks, both ALA and PBG are elevated at least 5-fold the upper limit of normal. The levels are high enough that a random urine sample is sufficient and a 24-hour urine collection is not recommended.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Normalise the spot urine ALA and PBG to creatinine; above 5 times the upper limit of normal is diagnostic. In ALAD porphyria only ALA is raised.**
claims.source_text: [Table 2. row 1] Diagnostic biochemical testing: Random urine PBG, ALA, and creatinine c … c Sample should be normalized to creatinine, levels should be >5-fold the upper limit of normal for diagnosis. In 5-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase only ALA is elevated.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not screen with urine porphyrins alone:** mild rises (secondary porphyrinuria) are often misread as porphyria and lead to overdiagnosis.
claims.source_text: Urine porphyrins should not be used alone as a screening test for AHP. Mild and nondiagnostic elevations in urinary porphyrins (secondary porphyrinurias) are often incorrectly interpreted as indicating AHP and lead to erroneous overdiagnosis.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Test during or soon after an attack.** Between attacks, 15%–44% of people with sporadic AIP have normal ALA and PBG, and levels can fall quickly in HCP and VP. In someone with frequent symptoms, normal ALA and PBG likely rule AHP out.
claims.source_text: When testing is performed in patients with sporadic AIP when they are asymptomatic, 15%-44% can have normal urine ALA and PBG values. … However, ALA and PBG levels can fall quickly after an acute attack in patients with HCP or VP. … In patients who have frequent symptoms suggestive of acute attacks, normal ALA and PBG levels likely rule out AHP as the etiology of the symptoms.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Confirm the type with genetic testing** (ALAD, HMBS, CPOX, PPOX) once biochemistry is positive, then offer testing to first-degree relatives. Genetics is not a first-line screen, because most carriers never have an attack.
claims.source_text: Best Practice Advice 3: Genetic testing should be used to confirm the diagnosis of AHP in patients with positive biochemical testing. … First-degree family members should be screened with genetic testing once the familial pathogenic variant has been identified in the patient with AHP to identify patients at risk for acute attacks. Those who are mutation carriers should be counseled. … Although genetic testing is the gold standard for confirmation of diagnosis, it is not recommended for initial screening. Most carriers of pathogenic variants in AHP genes do not experience symptomatic acute attacks in their lifetimes.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Attacks severe enough for admission: intravenous haem (hemin), 3–4 mg/kg once daily, typically for 4 days**, preferably into a high-flow central vein (PICC or port) because of thrombophlebitis.
claims.source_text: Best Practice Advice 4: Acute attacks of AHP that are severe enough to require hospital admission should be treated with intravenous hemin, given daily, preferably into a high-flow central vein. … usually given once daily at a dose of 3-4 mg/kg body weight, typically for 4 days. … Because of potential thrombophlebitis from hemin, it is best given into a high-flow central vein via a peripherally inserted central catheter or central port.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Collect the spot urine before the first haem dose.** In a patient with known AHP, haem can be started on clinical grounds without waiting for results.
claims.source_text: A random urine for ALA, PBG, and creatinine should be collected before the start of hemin treatment. … initiation of hemin can be made on empirical grounds in patients with confirmed AHP.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Supportive care:** stop precipitating drugs; treat pain and nausea aggressively; intravenous carbohydrate (about 300 g/day in adults) early in the attack; watch electrolytes and correct hyponatraemia slowly.
claims.source_text: Identifiable precipitating factors, such as medications that induce cytochrome P450s, should be stopped, as they can directly up-regulate ALAS1 messenger RNA. … Severe pain and nausea should be treated aggressively with analgesics and antiemetics. Intravenous carbohydrate loading (approximately 300 g/d in adults) … Electrolytes should be monitored during acute attacks and hyponatremia corrected slowly if present.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Seizures:** avoid barbiturates, hydantoins (phenytoin), carbamazepine and valproate. Magnesium sulfate, benzodiazepines and levetiracetam appear safe.
claims.source_text: many anticonvulsant medications, such as barbiturates, hydantoins, carbamazepine, and valproic acid, are contraindicated in AHP. Magnesium sulfate, benzodiazepines, and levetiracetam appear to be safe options in the context of AHP.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Advise every patient to avoid triggers:** alcohol, tobacco, fasting, stress, acute illness and cytochrome P450-inducing drugs. Progesterone is a known trigger. Check drug safety in the online porphyria drug databases.
claims.source_text: Sex hormones, in particular progesterone, are known to precipitate attacks. Other common precipitating factors include medications that induce cytochrome P450, acute illness or infection, physical or psychological stress, excess alcohol intake, tobacco use, and caloric deprivation. … All patients with AHP should be counseled to avoid identifiable triggers. Lists of safe and unsafe drugs are available online
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **With recurrent attacks (4 or more a year), consider outpatient prophylactic haem or givosiran.**
claims.source_text: Best Practice Advice 7: Prophylactic heme therapy or givosiran, administered in an outpatient setting, should be considered in patients with recurrent attacks (4 or more per year).
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prophylactic haem is off-label and less proven for prevention.** Long-term use brings central-line infections and iron overload, so screen for iron overload.
claims.source_text: Off-label use of prophylactic intravenous hemin infusion is common., Although hemin is effective at stopping acute attacks, its effectiveness in preventing recurrent attacks is less established. In addition, chronic hemin use is associated with several complications, including the need for indwelling central venous catheters, infections, and iron overload. Patients receiving prophylactic hemin therapy should be screened for iron overload
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Givosiran** (monthly subcutaneous siRNA against ALAS1) lowered attack rates in a phase 3 trial. Use it only when recurrent attacks are confirmed both biochemically and genetically, and not in pregnancy or when pregnancy is planned.
claims.source_text: In a phase 3, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled study of patients with AHP with recurrent attacks, monthly subcutaneous givosiran significantly lowered rates of acute attacks that correlated with lower urine ALA and PBG levels. … We suggest prescribing givosiran only for those patients with recurrent acute attacks that are both biochemically and genetically confirmed. Due to limited safety data, givosiran should not be used in women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitor on givosiran:** liver enzymes, urea and creatinine, homocysteine, amylase and lipase. Check liver enzymes monthly for the first 3–6 months (ALT rises above 3 times normal occur), then reduce to twice a year if normal.
claims.source_text: Patients on givosiran should be screened and monitored for elevations in liver enzymes, serum blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, homocysteine, amylase, and lipase. … Serum alanine aminotransferase elevation >3× the upper limit of normal has been reported in patients treated with givosiran during the first 3-6 months of treatment and, therefore, clinicians should monitor liver enzymes monthly during this period. If laboratory monitoring reveals normal findings, monitoring frequency may be decreased gradually to twice per year.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Givosiran laboratory panel (from the testing table):** comprehensive metabolic panel, plasma homocysteine, urinalysis, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, B12 and folate, amylase and lipase. Do it before the first dose and before each of the first 3 monthly injections; if stable and tolerated, every 3 months for the next year, then at least every 6 months.
claims.source_text: Monitoring on givosiran a , b: Comprehensive metabolic panel, plasma homocysteine urinalysis; urinary protein to creatinine ratio, B12/folate, amylase/lipase … b We recommend that the listed tests be performed before the start of givosiran and again just before each monthly injection of givosiran for 3 months. If the laboratory test results are stable and the drug is being well-tolerated, we recommend that laboratory monitoring be repeated once every 3 months for the next year and at least once every 6 months thereafter.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Menstrual-cycle attacks** can be treated with hormonal suppression such as a GnRH agonist, with limited success.
claims.source_text: Many patients are women who may experience menstrual cycle-associated attacks, which can be treated with hormonal suppression therapy, such as GnRH agonists, but with limited success.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Liver transplant only for intractable, drug-refractory disease** with badly reduced quality of life, ideally in an experienced centre. It has been curative in AIP. Screen related living donors genetically.
claims.source_text: Best Practice Advice 8: Liver transplantation for AHP should be limited to patients with intractable symptoms and significantly decreased quality of life who are refractory to pharmacotherapy. … If living donor transplantation is considered, genetic testing should be used to screen related living donors, as HMBS pathogenic variants in asymptomatic living donors may result in poor post-transplantation outcomes. … Transplantation should ideally be performed in centers with experience with AHP, including preoperative management with hemin.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Liver:** check liver enzymes at least yearly in treated patients. Abnormal results should prompt a search for other causes.
claims.source_text: Liver enzymes should be monitored at least annually in AHP patients actively undergoing treatment. … abnormal liver enzymes should prompt diagnostic investigation for alternative etiologies.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Annual monitoring list (from the testing table):** liver enzymes, creatinine and eGFR, and, from age 50, liver ultrasound with α-fetoprotein every 6 months.
claims.source_text: Annual Monitoring: Liver enzymes, creatinine and eGFR, liver ultrasound, and α -fetoprotein every 6 mo after age 50 y
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Iron on prophylactic haem (at least monthly):** check ferritin and iron every 3–6 months; consider venesection if ferritin is above 1000 ng/mL.
claims.source_text: In patients receiving prophylactic hemin therapy at least monthly, ferritin and iron levels should be monitored every 3-6 months. In patients with ferritin levels >1000 ng/mL, therapeutic phlebotomy should be considered to reduce iron overload.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **HCC surveillance from age 50 for everyone with AHP, whatever the symptoms:** liver ultrasound every 6 months. HCC can occur without cirrhosis.
claims.source_text: Best Practice Advice 10: Patients with AHP, regardless of the severity of symptoms, should undergo surveillance for HCC, beginning at age 50 years, with liver ultrasound every 6 months. … several studies have revealed that HCC may occur in the absence of liver fibrosis or cirrhosis.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Kidneys:** check creatinine and eGFR at least yearly, more often on givosiran (which may worsen eGFR in some), and control blood pressure. Kidney transplant is the treatment of choice for kidney failure due to AHP.
claims.source_text: serum creatinine and eGFR should be monitored at least annually in patients with AHP and more frequently in patients on givosiran. … therapeutic interventions, such as givosiran, may be associated with worsening eGFR and renal function in a subset of patients … Kidney transplantation is the treatment of choice for patients with end-stage renal disease secondary to AHP
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Counsel patients about long-term complications** (neuropathy, CKD, hypertension, HCC) and the need for lifelong monitoring. Asymptomatic high excretors may also need yearly monitoring.
claims.source_text: Best Practice Advice 12: Patients should be counseled on the chronic and long-term complications of AHP, including neuropathy, CKD, hypertension, and HCC, and need for long-term monitoring. … these patients may also experience an increased risk of CKD and HCC, and merit annual monitoring.
claims.locator: American Gastroenterological Association (Wang B, Bonkovsky HL, Lim JK, Balwani M), Gastroenterology, 'AGA Clinical Practice Update on Diagnosis and Management of Acute Hepatic Porphyrias: Expert Review', 2023, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10335308/, retrieved 2026-09-23
